sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The bird is a symbolic animal in Celtic thought. Celtic tradition presents birds as divine signs, as servants of the gods, and as their messengers. Birds often serve as marks or escorts of the goddesses. The Continental Celts carved bird figures in temples and stamped them on coins. Later Celtic narrative holds a rich store of bird symbolism. Early imagery links birds with the bull. Some Continental Celtic artists showed birds joined by silver chains. The carrion-eaters stand out most clearly. Crows and ravens accompanied goddesses of war and death. Irish legend casts the goddesses Badb, Macha, and Mórrígan at times as crows. The Irish hero Conaire could not kill birds. Irish tales tell of figures changed into birds: the Children of Lir, Cáer, and Angus Óg. The bird-headed Éis Enchenn fought Cúchulainn as a grotesque foe. Breton belief let the dead come back in bird shape. A Breton family killed and ate the enfant-oiseau, the infant-bird of Breton tale. The chough, called An Balores, stands as the emblem of Cornish identity. MacKillop lists many birds as important in the tradition, among them the crane, eagle, goose, and hawk. The bird is éan in Irish, eun in Scottish Gaelic, eean in Manx, and aderyn in Welsh.

okr.objective: Describe the bird as a divine symbol, messenger, and shape-changed figure across Celtic tradition.
key_results: Birds served the gods as divine signs, servants, and messengers.
The goddesses Badb, Macha, and Mórrígan appeared as crows, and Conaire could not kill birds.
